faq.q: What bedside sign suggests metabolic acidosis?

faq.a: Use Winter’s formula to predict expected PaCO₂; compare with observed respiratory rate.
faq.q: How do I estimate compensation for metabolic acidosis without ABG?

faq.a: Only if pH < 7.1, severe haemodynamic instability, or specific toxin ingestion.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with COPD presents with worsening dyspnoea; ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 70 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mmol/L — identify primary disorder and explain compensation.
A child with severe malaria develops deep breathing; bedside assessment suggests metabolic acidosis — which test confirms the diagnosis and what does a high anion gap indicate?
A patient on diuretics has vomiting and serum HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L; differentiate metabolic alkalosis from compensated respiratory acidosis.
In a low‑resource clinic you cannot obtain ABG; how would you use serum electrolytes and clinical signs to distinguish respiratory from metabolic acidosis?
A trauma patient receives massive blood transfusion and later shows pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L — interpret the disorder and appropriate immediate management.
Explain why giving a β‑agonist to a patient with severe metabolic acidosis from sepsis may be harmful.
A diabetic patient presents with Kussmaul breathing, glucose 450 mg/dL, urine ketones positive; outline the steps to correct the acid‑base disturbance.
Why is chronic respiratory alkalosis rarely seen in low‑resource settings, and what would be the expected bicarbonate level if it occurred?
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Understanding how the body maintains pH, the compensatory mechanisms, and how disturbances present clinically. Focus on low‑resource settings where arterial blood gas may be unavailable.

b: Normal pH: 7.35‑7.45
Normal PaCO₂: 35‑45 mmHg
Normal HCO₃⁻: 22‑26 mmol/L
sections.p: The body keeps arterial pH between 7.35‑7.45 using buffers, respiratory CO₂ control, and renal HCO₃⁻ handling.

b: Respiratory: ventilation changes PaCO₂ within minutes
Renal: HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, acid secretion, new HCO₃⁻ generation over hours
sections.p: Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) dissociates to CO₂ and H₂O; CO₂ is exhaled, HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed or generated by the kidneys.

b: Central chemoreceptors → CSF pH → medullary respiratory drive
Peripheral chemoreceptors → arterial O₂, pH, PaCO₂ → ventilation
sections.p: Chemoreceptors sense pH/PaCO₂ and adjust ventilation; kidneys respond to chronic changes via tubular transporters.

b: Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, opioid overdose)
Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation (e.g., anxiety, high altitude)
Metabolic acidosis: loss of HCO₃⁻ (diarrhoea) or acid accumulation (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, renal failure)
Metabolic alkalosis: HCO₃⁻ gain (vomiting, diuretic use)
sections.p: Acid‑base disorders arise from primary respiratory or metabolic disturbances, with compensation that may be incomplete.

b: Look for Kussmaul breathing (metabolic acidosis)
Observe rapid shallow breathing (respiratory alkalosis)
Check urine colour, anion gap, and clinical context
sections.p: Identify the primary disorder, assess compensation, and treat the underlying cause; in low‑resource settings use bedside clues when ABG is unavailable.

t.b: Determines primary disorder and compensation; if unavailable, use venous blood gas plus clinical signs
Identifies metabolic acidosis type; a gap >12 mmol/L suggests accumulation of unmeasured acids
Detects lactic acidosis in sepsis, malaria, severe anaemia
Confirms ketoacidosis in diabetic or alcoholic patients
Detects pneumonia or pulmonary oedema causing respiratory acidosis

b: Respiratory acidosis: improve ventilation (e.g., bronchodilators, CPAP, treat obstruction)
Respiratory alkalosis: treat underlying hyperventilation, give anxiolytics if needed
Metabolic acidosis: give IV fluids, treat sepsis, give insulin for DKA, consider sodium bicarbonate only if pH <7.1 or haemodynamic collapse
Metabolic alkalosis: replace chloride, stop diuretics, give isotonic saline
sections.p: Treat the cause first; provide supportive ventilation or fluids; correct severe pH only if life‑threatening.

b: Chronic respiratory acidosis vs. metabolic alkalosis (both raise HCO₃⁻)
Ketoacidosis vs. lactic acidosis (both high anion gap)
sections.p: Distinguish primary from compensated disorders; e.g., chronic COPD respiratory acidosis may have near‑normal pH due to renal compensation.

b: Low bicarbonate with normal PaCO₂ may be early metabolic acidosis before compensation
High anion gap with normal lactate suggests other acids (e.g., renal failure, toxins)
sections.p: Venous pH is ~0.03‑0.04 lower than arterial; a normal venous pH may hide arterial acidosis.

b: Always state primary disorder, compensation, and whether compensation is appropriate
Use the Winter’s formula (expected PaCO₂ = 1.5×[HCO₃⁻] + 8 ±2) for metabolic acidosis compensation
Remember that chronic respiratory acidosis raises HCO₃⁻ by ~4 mmol/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PaCO₂
